title: Design Systems That Hold Without Being Watched
subtitle: Tokens, enforcement and governance — and what happens to a shared system when nobody reports to you

cv.note: Tailored for the Lead Design Systems role

bio.short: I build design systems and the machinery that keeps them honest. Tokens in three tiers, one commit reaching every platform, and a build that refuses work which leaves the system.
bio.long:
I build design systems. The last year went into the part most systems skip: the layer that makes the standard hold when nobody is checking.

At Bibel TV the tokens ship as an API. Three tiers, from global primitives through semantic to component, so one commit reaches Figma, Android and web at once. Primitives are fixed. Semantics are the contract. Component tokens are where a product team gets room. Standardization and flexibility are held apart by architecture rather than by policy.

Above that sits the enforcement. Six checks run identically on a laptop and in CI. Two were written against mistakes I watched an AI assistant make. One is a token reference that does not resolve, the other a colour hardcoded into a component. Both compile and both render, which is why review never catches them. Run over a library already cleaned twice, they identified 32 values that had drifted off-system.

Accessibility sits inside the same instinct, and the ChurchDesk work is the part I would point at. We audited our own website and also the websites customers build with the platform, for EU Accessibility Act compliance. The second half is the harder one. Those sites are made by parish staff, not by specialists, so the standard has to hold in output nobody trained for. I shipped AI alt-text generation there too, for EU accessibility compliance across six countries. Screen-reader semantics and ARIA are standing practice for me, at Bibel TV as well as ChurchDesk and Ninox.

The colour engine is the same idea one layer down. K-means clustering in OKLCH rather than RGB, so themes carry even perceptual weight. WCAG contrast is validated inside the algorithm, so no theme can ship failing. Every threshold is a dial in a config tool rather than a commit.

What I would bring to a shared design foundation is that combination. Token architecture, a build that refuses to compromise it, and enough governance that people extend the system rather than route around it.

It is also the version of design leadership I have most practice at. The influence comes from what the system makes easy. At Bibel TV it holds across a handoff to an external engineering agency, which is a harder test than an internal team.

context.emphasis: Token architecture and the enforcement layer first, because T4, T7, T9 and T11 are the bulk of this posting. Then influence without a reporting line, which T5 and T15 ask for as the job itself rather than as a bonus. Accessibility as a practice rather than as two artifacts, widened 2026-08-17. The ChurchDesk audit is the lead: it covered the company website and the websites customers build with the platform, for EU Accessibility Act compliance. Then screen-reader semantics and ARIA across three companies, alt-text shipped under EU compliance, and contrast held in the algorithm. Mentoring shown as a decade of it, which is unusual and directly answers T15.
